appraisal_events.evidence: "Supportez d'être appelée une nerveuse. Vous appartenez à cette famille magnifique et lamentable qui est le sel de la terre. Tout ce que nous connaissons de grand nous vient des nerveux"; "Et vous ne vous trompiez pas, vous les aviez"; and the closing demonstration, "elle a commencé à vous guérir, vous m'écoutez toute droite, sans vous être appuyée une fois, l'œil vif, la mine bonne, et il y a de cela une demi-heure d'horloge".
appraisal_events.explanation: The doctor converts the grandmother's discredited nervous complaints into a title of honour — the affliction of the poets and founders of religions, her symptoms real rather than imagined — and closes by showing her already standing straight under his word; her one objection is absorbed and turned back on her.

status_effects.explanation: She passes from a woman suspected of imaginary illness to one whose sufferings are affirmed as real and as the price of everything great; even her fear is credited rather than mocked.

The doctor formally enrolls her in a named company — "cette famille magnifique et lamentable qui est le sel de la terre" — alongside the greatest poet of the age and, by his reciprocal confession, himself.

He holds the floor for half an hour, dissolves her objection that she is nothing like the cloistered cousin, disarms suspicion by confessing his own manias, and ends by producing the proof of his own effect before taking his leave.

ambiguities: The doctor is designated in the passage only as "le docteur" and "Monsieur"; he is resolved to du Boulbon as the nerve specialist consulted about the grandmother's illness and the friend of Bergotte named in the preceding context.

The narration notes that the grandmother raises her objections "dans l'espoir qu'il les réfuterait", so that the consolation she receives is one she has invited, which qualifies how far the passage stands behind the doctor's happy diagnosis.
